summary:
São Paulo state stands under Brazil's national framework, which is applied uniformly across all 27 states. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since May 2013 under National Council of Justice Resolution 175/2013, binding on every civil registry after a 14-1 vote, and joint adoption has been available since 2015. Name and gender-marker changes require no surgery, spousal-visa equality operates on the same footing as for any other traveller, and lesbian, gay and bisexual people serve openly in the armed forces. A trans visitor's documents and status are therefore handled on the ordinary terms at entry and in family matters.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court ruled in ADO 26 that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is a crime equivalent to racism under Lei 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. Transphobia is prosecuted on that footing, and the provision has been applied to commercial conduct inside the state: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing, affirming the compensation ordered at first instance in Barra Bonita. A visitor who faces discriminatory conduct in São Paulo can invoke the same provision.

No specific federal anti-discrimination statute exists; the protection rests on the 2019 ruling and constitutional provisions, and repeal efforts have been tabled in Congress. In 2023 the Superior Court of Justice allowed non-binary people to amend their civil records, while intersex people have no specific legal protections.

The protective text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions. A May 2024 investigation documented 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo nightlife, in a city that hosts Pride events drawing thousands of tourists.

Arrest carries a specific and contested regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. A person is recognised as LGBTI by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing; the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units, ask trans, travesti and intersex people their preference, and record it in a reasoned decision. Placement can be changed later, transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat, LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census carried out between April and June 2021 in Rio de Janeiro state prisons interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine, and documents that travestis and trans women are held in masculine-operated units, with some placed in so-called neutral or security units; it treats placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. Comparable national norms from 2014 and 2020 permit people to be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine.
tangentialFactors:
Social friction varies by setting. Larger Brazilian cities carry legal infrastructure such as specialist counsel and established advocacy organisations, while smaller cities and rural areas carry more social friction; São Paulo city concentrates both the strongest support network and, as the May 2024 investigation shows, documented nightlife targeting of LGBTQIA+ people.

The country's violence-prevention statutes have been extended toward trans women. An analysis of case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women.

Political visibility carries an accompanying risk. In the October 2024 municipal elections close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state of the country and received death threats and intimidation, while the number of trans officeholders tripled compared with the previous cycle.

Brazil's record is a useful regional comparator: it combines broad statutory protection with documented non-enforcement, a pattern that repeats in neighbouring jurisdictions where formal equality has outpaced practice.
localsOnly:
Residents may change their legal name and gender marker without surgery, and since a 2023 ruling of the Superior Court of Justice non-binary people may amend their civil records to reflect a non-binary status.

Same-sex couples have had access to marriage since 2013 and to joint adoption since 2015, with spousal benefits and visas on equal terms. Lesbian, gay and bisexual people may serve openly in the armed forces.

Discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds have been criminally prohibited since the 2019 Supreme Federal Court ruling, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism, and that protection applies to employment, services and public accommodation as well as to entry of venues. No consolidated federal anti-discrimination statute exists, and repeal efforts have been put to Congress, so the protection depends on the constitutional and criminal provisions rather than on dedicated legislation.

Intersex people have no specific legal protections, and people who are arrested or detained are entitled to have their placement decided by a judge after consultation, with their declared preference recorded and LGBTI-specific units not usable for disciplinary isolation.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory documents how National Council of Justice Resolution 348/366 is applied in São Paulo state's own prison units, whether placement matches declared preference, or whether LGBTI-specific spaces are used for isolation here. The Rio de Janeiro census is cited as the available evidence of practice in a Brazilian prison system and is not a finding about São Paulo.

The scope of the 2023 non-binary record-amendment ruling — whether it requires a court application, which documents are needed, and how it interacts with passport and foreign-document conventions — is not sourced here.

Intersex-specific protections, including any rules on medical interventions, are stated to be absent at national level but are not separately documented for São Paulo state.

The status and any parliamentary progress of the repeal efforts mentioned in the 2026 country overview are unresolved in this inventory.

São Paulo-specific incident data on hate-crime reporting rates, police response, or outcomes of complaints brought under Lei 7.716/1989 in the state is not sourced.
